title: Connection Lab
intro: Practice conversation, dating, and relationship skills through short, fictional choices. There is no perfect script or guaranteed outcome.
privacy: Your practice choices and personal stories are not saved here. Usage analytics records lesson IDs and scene counts, not the response you picked. Skip freely.
timeboxHint_one: Plan for {{count}} minute. No countdown or reminder starts.
timeboxHint_other: Plan for {{count}} minutes. No countdown or reminder starts.
practiced: You tried {{done}} of {{total}} choices. Skipped steps carry no penalty.

feedback.strong: This choice respects the other person's agency and leaves space for a reply.
feedback.mixed: This could work in some contexts. Notice the other person's cues and make room for their perspective.
feedback.pressuring: This risks pressure, dismissal, or crossing a boundary. Try a clearer and more respectful option.

approach.title: Approach and start
approach.goal: Open with context, curiosity, and an easy exit.
approach.evidence: Adapted from question-asking studies; these studies do not test a universal opening line.
approach.transfer: Tiny real-world step: greet someone in a low-stakes setting. No need to extend the exchange.

open.prompt: At a community event, someone is reading the activity schedule.
open.tip: A context-based opener gives the other person an easy choice to engage or not.

a.text: Hi! Have you tried any of these activities?
a.response: They might say, 'Yes, I liked the last one.'

b.text: This place is great. Let me tell you all about my week.
b.response: They might listen briefly, without much room to join in.

c.text: You should stop looking at that and talk to me.
c.response: They might turn away or feel uncomfortable.

follow.prompt: They smile and say, 'I'm waiting for a friend.'
follow.tip: Sometimes the best continuation is a warm exit.

a.text: I'll keep you company until they arrive.
a.response: They might feel obligated to continue.

b.text: Got it. Hope you both enjoy the event!
b.response: They might smile and return to their plans.

c.text: Then give me your number before they get here.
c.response: They might feel pushed after explaining their situation.

flow.title: Keep conversation flowing
flow.goal: Listen, ask a meaningful follow-up, and share a little of yourself.
flow.evidence: Follow-up questions were linked to liking in conversation studies; the speed-dating analysis has published critiques and a reply.
flow.transfer: Tiny step: ask one follow-up question about something someone already mentioned.

listen.prompt: Someone says, 'I started going on short hikes recently.'
listen.tip: Follow-ups show attention; don't turn the exchange into an interview.

a.text: I hike all the time. Here is my entire gear list.
a.response: They might lose their chance to tell their story.

b.text: Hiking is pointless. You should try the gym.

c.text: What got you interested in hiking?
c.response: They might share what motivated them.

share.prompt: They add, 'I prefer easy trails and good views.'
share.tip: Combine a brief personal detail with genuine curiosity.

a.text: I like easy walks too. Have you found a favorite view?
a.response: They might name a trail and ask about yours.

b.text: That's boring. Hard trails are the only real hikes.

c.response: They might pause, unsure where to go next.

flirt.title: Express interest respectfully
flirt.goal: Show romantic interest clearly without assuming it is returned.
flirt.evidence: Attraction between specific people is difficult to predict from traits; these invitation scripts are practice heuristics, not validated formulas.
flirt.transfer: Tiny step: write one invitation that makes yes and no equally easy. You do not have to send it.

interest.prompt: After an art class, you enjoyed chatting with someone and would like to meet again.
interest.tip: Be specific and easy to decline. A friendly exchange is not consent to a date.

a.text: You owe me a date after that conversation.

b.text: I enjoyed talking with you. Would you like coffee sometime? No pressure.
b.response: They might accept, decline, or ask for time.

c.response: They might appreciate it, or find it too personal for the setting.

unclear.prompt: They reply, 'Maybe. This week is busy.'
unclear.tip: Uncertainty is not a yes. Leave control of the next step with them.

a.text: I'll keep messaging until you pick a day.
a.response: They might feel pursued despite their hesitation.

b.text: No worries. If you want to, let me know.
b.response: They might appreciate the space, regardless of what happens next.

c.response: They might clarify, or feel pushed to decide now.

connect.title: Build emotional connection
connect.goal: Offer attention and gradual, mutual sharing without forcing intimacy.
connect.evidence: Structured mutual disclosure increased short-term closeness in one experimental comparison. It does not guarantee romance or long-term connection.
connect.transfer: Tiny step: ask someone you trust whether they want listening, advice, or a distraction.

disclose.prompt: A friend says, 'It's been a hard week.'
disclose.tip: Support starts with the kind of help they want, not forced disclosure.

a.text: That sounds tiring. Want to talk, or would a distraction help?
a.response: They might choose what feels comfortable.

b.response: They might feel pressured to reveal more than they want.

c.response: They might feel their experience was minimized.

support.prompt: They answer, 'I don't want to get into it.'
support.tip: Respecting a no can strengthen trust more than asking for details.

a.text: I'm sure you'll feel better if you vent.
a.response: They might repeat that they do not want to talk.

b.text: Okay. I'm here if that changes.
b.response: They might feel understood and free to decide later.

c.text: Why don't you trust me enough to tell me?
c.response: They might feel blamed for having a boundary.

rejection.title: Confidence and rejection
rejection.goal: Respond to a no with dignity and recover without self-judgment.
rejection.evidence: CBT helps many people with anxiety disorders; this short non-clinical practice is not a treatment or a tested rejection intervention.
rejection.transfer: Tiny step: write one kind sentence you can tell yourself after an awkward interaction.

no.prompt: You invite someone to meet and they say, 'Thanks, but no.'
no.tip: A clear no ends the invitation. You can still be warm.

a.text: Why not? Just give me a chance.
a.response: They might feel their answer was not respected.

b.text: But we get along so well!
b.response: They might feel they need to defend their decision.

c.text: Thanks for letting me know. Take care.
c.response: They might appreciate the straightforward response.

reset.prompt: Afterward, you feel disappointed and start replaying the moment.
reset.tip: Focus on the actions you control; other people's choices are not a score.

a.text: Take a short break and return to something meaningful to you.
a.response: You might regain perspective with time.

b.text: Analyze every word until you find the mistake.
b.response: You might get stuck in an unhelpful loop.

c.text: Find another way to change their mind.
c.response: You might cross a boundary already made clear.

repair.title: Repair and stay connected
repair.goal: Listen to a concern, take responsibility, and agree on a specific next step.
repair.evidence: Responsiveness is an established relationship framework. These exact scripts have not been tested as an intervention.
repair.transfer: Tiny step: practice saying, 'I see why that mattered to you. What would help next time?'

listen.prompt: Your partner says, 'I felt unheard when we planned our weekend.'
listen.tip: Understand the concern before defending your intention.

a.text: I was busy too, you know.
a.response: They might feel you missed their concern.

b.text: I missed that. What felt most frustrating?
b.response: They might explain a specific moment.

c.response: They might feel dismissed or withdraw.

repair.prompt: They ask, 'Can we make the next plan together?'
repair.tip: Repair works better with a concrete, mutually acceptable next step.

a.response: They might doubt the agreement is sincere.

b.response: They might not know what will change.

c.text: Yes. Can we choose a time and each share our priorities?
c.response: They might agree to a workable plan.
